question.text: Assertion: For a projectile, if you pick any two positions along its path with velocities v₁, v₂ occurring at times t₁, t₂, the ratio (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) always works out to the same value. Reason: This ratio is the average acceleration, and it stays fixed because the acceleration of the projectile does not change.

options.1: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.2: If both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.
options.3: If the Assertion is true, but the Reason is false.
options.4: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

conditions: v₁, v₂ are the velocities at two positions during projectile motion
t₁, t₂ are the corresponding times

solution.approach: The ratio of the change in velocity to the change in time between any two instants is by definition the average acceleration, which equals the constant acceleration in projectile motion.

steps.text: Write the definition of average acceleration between two instants of time.
In projectile motion the acceleration is constant and equal to g downward at every instant, with no other force acting.
Since the instantaneous acceleration never changes, the average acceleration between any two chosen instants must also equal this same constant value.
So the ratio (v₂ − v₁)/(t₂ − t₁) always equals g downward, whichever two positions are chosen, and the Reason correctly names this ratio as the average acceleration, which is why it stays constant.
steps.why_this_step: The Reason states the definition that directly explains why the Assertion holds for any pair of instants.

final_answer.value: If both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the ratio changes with the chosen positions because velocity itself keeps changing throughout the flight.
Accepting both statements as true but treating the Reason as a separate fact rather than the definition that directly explains the Assertion.
